Withs
withz
n. pl. (pliant twigs or cords of green willow, used as bonds; the first of Delilah's four attempts on Samson)
From Old English withthe, a willow twig, related to withy, the willow itself. The Hebrew is yether, a cord or bowstring — the margin of the Authorized Version notes the alternative rendering new cords, and the Hebrew adds lachim, moist or fresh.

Biblical Definition

Withs are green, unseasoned willow cords, and their strength is proverbial — a fresh withy binds where a dry one snaps. The word occurs three times, all in one episode. Samson tells Delilah: “If they bind me with seven green withs that were never dried, then shall I be weak, and be as another man” (Judges 16:7). She acts on it at once: “Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven green withs which had not been dried, and she bound him with them” (Judges 16:8). And the outcome: “he brake the withs, as a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire. So his strength was not known” (Judges 16:9). The number seven and the specification never dried give the lie a ritual air, as though Samson were inventing a plausible superstition; but the reader should notice what the episode really discloses. Delilah had already told him plainly what she wanted — to know wherewith he might be bound to afflict him — and there were armed men in the room. He kept coming back. The withs failed; the pattern of returning to the thing that was hunting him did not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines with or withe as a twig or flexible branch, particularly of willow, used as a band or rope.

WITHE, n. A willow twig; a flexible twig used as a band.

2. A band consisting of a twig, or of twigs twisted.

If they bind me with seven green withs. Judges 16.

WITHY, n. The willow, or a large species of willow.

BAND, n. A fillet; a cord; a tie; a chain; any narrow ligament with which a thing is bound.

Key Scripture

Judges 16:7 — "And Samson said unto her, If they bind me with seven green withs that were never dried, then shall I be weak, and be as another man."

Judges 16:8 — "Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven green withs which had not been dried, and she bound him with them."

Judges 16:9 — "Now there were men lying in wait, abiding with her in the chamber. And she said unto him, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he brake the withs, as a thread of tow is broken when it toucheth the fire. So his strength was not known."

Proverbs 7:22 — "He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks;"

Modern Corruption

The episode is read as a story about a woman's deceit, when the narrative's weight falls on a man who saw the trap plainly and returned to it.

expand to see more

Retellings of Judges 16 concentrate on Delilah, and the moral drawn is generally a warning about treacherous women. That is not where the narrator puts the emphasis. Delilah's intention is stated openly in verse 6, before any of the four attempts, and the armed men are in the chamber. Samson is not deceived about her purpose at any point; he is simply unwilling to leave. This is the anatomy of besetting sin that Proverbs describes at length — the young man void of understanding going the way to her house, knowing the way and going it — and the Authorized Version's own comparison is a beast walking to the slaughter.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that knowledge is not deliverance. Samson could have written an accurate account of his danger and did in fact break every bond they tried, which only prolonged the arrangement and deepened the trust that he was invulnerable. The four attempts are recorded so that the reader watches a man survive three warnings and lose on the fourth. Whatever a man can break repeatedly, he will eventually stop being able to break; the withs held nothing, and the habit held everything.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yether, a cord or bowstring — Judges 16:7-9; lach, moist or fresh — the green, undried quality; Old English withthe, a willow twig.

expand to see more

Hebrew yether — a cord, string, or bowstring; the word rendered withs in Judges 16.

Hebrew lach — moist, fresh, green; the specification that they were never dried.

Hebrew asar — to bind; the verb used of every attempt on Samson.

Hebrew shibah — seven; the number Samson specified, giving the lie a ritual sound.

Old English withthe, a willow twig, whence withy — the source of the English word.

Usage

"“Seven green withs that were never dried” — the first of four false answers."

"“So his strength was not known” — and he stayed in the room."

"The narrative's weight is on the man who returned, not the woman who asked."
